passages.where: Ezekiel speaks against the shepherds of Israel, its rulers, who fed themselves while the flock went hungry, sick and scattered. God names what they failed to do, strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, search for the lost, and what they did instead: they ruled with violence and cruelty. Scripture does not treat harm done by the people charged with care as a small thing.

After the charge comes a promise. God says he will shepherd his flock himself: seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak. The site's note on the chapter adds that he will judge between the strong sheep who trample the pasture and the weak, and shepherd them with justice.

The psalmist could have endured an enemy's insults. What breaks him is that the attack comes from a close friend, one he walked with into the house of God. The site's plain note says a friend's betrayal hurts more than an enemy's attack, that this is true, and that the pain is not an overreaction.

Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples about teachers who tie heavy loads on other people's shoulders and will not lift a finger to move them. The site's note sets the picture against his own invitation, whose burden is light. Its plain note says the warning lands first on those who teach and lead in his church today.

Jesus invites everyone worn out by their load to come to him, and calls himself gentle and humble in heart. The site's plain note says many people have heard the invitation as one more demand, and that it is spoken to anyone worn out by a kind of religion that felt like a weight they could never lift. A yoke is made for two, and the one beside you is kind.

Jesus calls himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep, and contrasts himself with the hired hand who runs when the wolf comes because he does not care for them. The site's plain note speaks to anyone hurt by shepherds who fed themselves: God condemned those shepherds, and Jesus defined a true one as a shepherd who gives his life for the sheep, not one who takes life from them. Your hurt does not mean God was like them.

A man born blind has been healed, and when he insists that the one who healed him must be from God, the authorities call him born in sin and throw him out. The site's note says they used sin as a weapon, a label for someone else. Then Jesus hears what they have done and goes to find him, and the plain note says that anyone put out by a church, a family or a town can remember that Jesus went looking for the man they threw out.

Jesus has just set a child among his disciples. The site's note calls this the most severe warning in the Gospels, aimed at anyone who causes a little one who believes in him to stumble, and its plain note says the words have rightly been applied to the abuse of children. The church has sometimes protected abusers and silenced children, the note says, and that is a betrayal of this very passage.

Paul tells the elders of the church at Ephesus that savage wolves will come in among them, and that men from their own number will distort the truth to draw disciples after themselves. Scripture expected harm to come from inside the church, not only from outside it. The site's plain note says such people may speak from the front of a church.

Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first, slanders the elder, refuses to welcome traveling believers, and puts out of the church those who want to. The elder names the wrong plainly and plans to deal with it openly, without answering slander with slander. The site's plain note says the letter does not ask anyone to stay under a leader who controls, shames or harms them.

A hymn sets God's power over the stars beside his care for the lowly: the one who counts the stars and calls them by name heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. The site's plain note says he is not too big to notice you.

misread.taken: “Why not rather be wronged?” and the verses around it, about believers going to law before unbelievers, are used to tell someone harmed in a church not to go to the police, or to keep a crime inside the church so that it can be settled quietly.
misread.says: The site's plain note answers plainly: Paul is speaking of everyday civil disputes between believers, over money, property and business, “trivial cases” in his words, not of crimes. Nothing here tells anyone to keep a crime hidden or to settle it quietly inside the church. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul himself calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4), and Paul used the Roman courts when he needed to (Acts 25:11). His anger in this chapter is aimed at the strong who cheated the weak, not at the weak who sought help.

whole: If someone in a church abused you, or a crime was done, or you are still in danger, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust outside that church, take a crime to the police, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Church hurt comes in more than one shape. It may have been a pastor who could not be questioned, who treated your doubts as rebellion. It may have been abuse by a leader or a volunteer, and then a second blow when the people in charge protected the one who did it. It may have been a congregation that closed ranks when you spoke, or friends who disappeared the month you divorced or fell sick. Afterward a parking lot on a Sunday morning can make you want to keep driving, and the verses that were used on you can still sound like the voice that used them.

Scripture is not surprised by any of this, and it is not neutral. Ezekiel's shepherds fed themselves and ruled the flock with violence. Jesus saved some of his sharpest words for teachers who laid heavy loads on others and would not lift a finger, and the site's note on Matthew 23 says that warning lands first on those who lead in his church today. Paul told the elders at Ephesus that wolves would rise from their own number, and the elder who wrote to Gaius named a leader who loved to be first and put faithful people out of the church. What makes church hurt cut so deep is that it comes from people who spoke for God, so the wound reaches past them toward God himself, and many who carry it are left asking whether any of it was real. When shepherds harm the flock, Scripture puts God against them, not beside them.

So the first wisdom is to tell the truth about what happened, to God and to one safe person, without softening it to sound more spiritual. The site's notes are plain: what a controlling leader or church did to you was wrong and not your fault, you are free to step away, and a crime belongs with the authorities, not only with the church. Ordinary disappointment among sinners is one thing; using God's name or a leader's place to control someone, to silence them, or to shield the one who did harm is another. Take the time you need, and do not let the people who hurt you decide whether you keep Jesus: he went looking for the man they threw out. When you are ready, a pastor or counselor outside that church can help you sort out what happened, and a church worth trusting is one where leaders can be questioned and a hurt person is believed.

The hope Scripture gives is not that the church will stop failing people. It is that God has not left his flock to the shepherds who failed it. In Ezekiel he promises to seek the lost, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak himself, and to judge between the strong sheep who trample the pasture and the weak. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and invites everyone worn out by a heavy religion to come to one who is gentle and humble in heart. The God who calls the stars by name binds up wounds, and yours are not too small for him to see.
sit: What did the people who hurt you teach you to believe about God, and what does Jesus, who went looking for the man they threw out, say instead?

prayer.lead: After the shepherds who fed themselves, the psalm names the one who does not. The site's plain note says its promise is not that the sheep will never be in danger, but that the shepherd will never leave.

careLines.text: If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault.
You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust.
If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities.
If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now.
A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
